newsitem.title: UK: Russia's limits on '97 bond supply boost prices.
newsitem.headline: Russia's limits on '97 bond supply boost prices.

text.p: News on Monday that Russia might cancel plans for another Eurobond in 1997 calmed fears of oversupply and prices of the country's two outstanding dollar bonds rose.
Deputy finance minister Mikhail Kasyanov said tax collection was rising and Russia might not issue another Eurobond in 1997.
"It is healthy to limit the supply as investors were beginning to worry that Russia might borrow itself into oblivion," a debt analyst said.
One banker said: "It's always good news for bond holders when a borrower says it has completed its funding for the year."

Russia's $1.0 billion November 2001 bond was bid at an historical low of 247 basis points over U.S. Treasury notes versus levels of around 251 b.p. last week and a launch spread last November of 345 b.p.
Its $2.0 billion June 2007 bond was bid at around 343 b.p. versus 346 b.p. last week and a launch spread of 375 b.p. in June, dealers said.

"We would expect the deals to tighten further. Anything that leads to a limited amount of bonds from the region causes a scarcity effect which is positive for other Russian borrowers," A Deutsche Bank official in Frankfurt said.

Russia has raised a total of $4.1 billion on the international bond markets since November last year and had plans to launch a global bond later this year. Bankers had estimated the size of the offering would be up to $1.0 billion.

Bankers said Russia's extensive borrowing could inhibit other borrowers from the country from raising money. There is a long list of banks, corporates and regions wanting to come to market. They said that this announcement might clear the way for these issuers.
So far the only non-sovereign Russian borrowers have been the cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.
"If a sovereign borrows money too frequently, it crowds out other borrowing from the country, like Russia might have done," an analyst said.
Besides the two dollar bonds, Russia also has one mark bond outstanding. The 2.0 billion mark ($1.1 billion) 2004 bond was launched in March this year.

"There is overall investor confidence in Russia. We just see a lot of demand," a banker said, adding there was also speculation Russia might be upgraded this year from its current Ba2/BB- ratings from Moody's Investors Service and Standard & Poor's.

A Russian State Tax Service official said tax collection in the first five months was 85 percent of the budget forecast, after 69 percent in the first quarter. She said June tax collection was even better, but the exact figure was not yet available.
